prompt: Some people think that schools should teach practical life skills, such as managing money and cooking, instead of academic subjects like history and literature. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
text:
It is often argued that schools should replace academic subjects such as history and literature with practical life skills like budgeting and cooking. While I agree that these skills deserve a place in the curriculum, I do not believe they should replace traditional subjects entirely.

On the one hand, there are clear reasons to teach practical skills. Many young adults leave school without knowing how to create a budget, use a bank account responsibly or understand interest on a loan. As a result, some of them fall into debt soon after they start working. Similarly, cooking is a skill that affects health every day, and students who can prepare simple meals are less likely to depend on unhealthy fast food. Because of this, it would be reasonable for schools to spend some time on these topics.

On the other hand, academic subjects develop abilities that practical lessons cannot. Studying history helps students to understand how societies change and why conflicts happen, which makes them more informed citizens. Literature, meanwhile, improves reading comprehension, vocabulary and the ability to understand other peoples feelings. These skills are useful in almost every career, even if they are not obviously practical.

In my view, the best solution is to combine both approaches. Schools could include a short course on personal finance and basic cooking in the final years, without removing history and literature from the timetable.

In conclusion, although practical life skills are valuable and should be taught, they should be added to the curriculum rather than replacing academic subjects that also prepare students for adult life.

prompt: Some people think that schools should teach practical life skills, such as managing money and cooking, instead of academic subjects like history and literature. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
text:
There is a growing view that schools should prioritise practical competencies, such as budgeting and cooking, over traditional disciplines like history and literature. Although I accept that many school leavers are poorly prepared for the everyday demands of adult life, I strongly disagree that the solution is to sacrifice academic subjects.

The case for practical education is easy to understand. Young people are increasingly exposed to credit cards, online loans and subscription services long before they have any grasp of interest rates or household budgeting, and the consequences of this ignorance can follow them for years. Likewise, an inability to cook leaves many students reliant on processed food, with obvious implications for their long-term health. It would therefore be negligent for schools to ignore these areas altogether.

Nevertheless, framing this as a choice between practical and academic learning is misleading. History does far more than recount dates; it trains students to weigh conflicting sources, recognise propaganda and understand how present-day institutions came into being. Literature, for its part, cultivates empathy and the capacity to follow complex arguments, both of which underpin effective communication in any profession. These are, in a deeper sense, highly practical skills, even if their value is less immediately visible than that of a cooking lesson.

Moreover, the skills in question do not require a large share of the timetable. A focused module on personal finance, perhaps integrated into mathematics, and a short course in basic nutrition could be delivered without displacing subjects that take years to master.

In conclusion, while schools should certainly equip pupils to manage money and feed themselves, this goal can be achieved alongside, rather than at the expense of, the academic subjects that shape thoughtful and well-informed adults.

prompt: Some people believe that the best way to reduce traffic in cities is to make public transport free. Others think that this money should be spent on building better roads. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
text:
Traffic congestion has become a serious issue in most large cities. While some people argue that offering free public transport is the most effective solution, others believe that the same funds should be invested in improving the road network. This essay will examine both views before explaining why I support the first option.

Supporters of free public transport point out that cost is one of the main reasons people choose private vehicles. If buses and trains were free, commuters who currently drive short distances would have a strong incentive to leave their cars at home. This would not only reduce the number of vehicles on the road but also lower air pollution, which is a major health concern in crowded urban areas.

Those who prefer investing in roads argue that the real problem is poor infrastructure. Narrow roads, badly planned junctions and a lack of flyovers create bottlenecks, and fixing these could allow traffic to flow more smoothly. In addition, better roads benefit everyone, including people in suburbs and rural areas who have limited access to public transport.

However, I believe that building more roads only provides a temporary solution. Experience in many cities shows that wider roads tend to attract more cars, so congestion soon returns to its previous level. Free public transport, on the other hand, addresses the cause of the problem by changing the way people travel, although it must be combined with more frequent and reliable services to be successful.

In conclusion, both approaches have some merit, but making public transport free is likely to have a more lasting impact on urban traffic.

prompt: Some people believe that the best way to reduce traffic in cities is to make public transport free. Others think that this money should be spent on building better roads. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
text:
How to tackle urban congestion is a question that divides opinion. One camp maintains that abolishing fares on public transport would persuade drivers to abandon their cars, whereas another insists that public money would be better spent upgrading roads. Having considered both positions, I am more persuaded by the case for free public transport, provided it is accompanied by investment in service quality.

The argument for road building rests largely on capacity. Many cities in developing countries still rely on road networks designed for a fraction of today's vehicles, and poorly designed intersections can bring entire districts to a standstill. Widening key routes and adding ring roads would, in principle, allow traffic to move more freely, while also serving residents of outlying areas who have no realistic alternative to driving.

Advocates of free public transport, however, focus on demand rather than supply. They argue that as long as driving remains convenient and public transport costs money, commuters will continue to choose cars, and additional lanes will simply fill up again. This phenomenon, often called induced demand, has been observed repeatedly, which suggests that road expansion offers only short-lived relief. Removing fares, by contrast, directly lowers the cost of the alternative, and cities that have experimented with this policy have reported noticeable increases in ridership.

In my view, the second argument is more convincing, but fare abolition alone is not enough. If buses are slow, unreliable or overcrowded, people will not switch regardless of the price. Free travel should therefore be combined with dedicated bus lanes and more frequent services.

In conclusion, although better roads may ease congestion temporarily, making public transport free and attractive is the more sustainable long-term strategy.

prompt: Some people say that working from home is better for employees than working in an office. Do you agree or disagree? Support your opinion with reasons and examples. Write 200-300 words.
text:
In recent years, working from home has become very common, especially after the pandemic. Some people think it is better for employees than working in an office. In my opinion, I mostly agree with this statement for the following reasons.

Firstly, working from home saves a lot of time and money. Employees do not need to travel to the office every day, so they can avoid traffic jams and spend the extra time with their family or on their hobbies. For example, a person who travels two hours every day can save around forty hours in a month.

Secondly, many employees feel more comfortable and productive at home. They can choose a quiet place and organise their day in their own way. Studies has shown that some workers complete more tasks when they are not disturbed by colleagues.

However, working from home also have some disadvantages. Some people feel lonely and it is difficult to communicate with the team. Also young employees may not learn as quickly because they cannot watch experienced colleagues.

In conclusion, although there are some problems, I believe that working from home is generally better for employees because it gives them more time, flexibility and comfort. Companies should consider allowing employees to work from home at least a few days in a week.

prompt: Some people say that working from home is better for employees than working in an office. Do you agree or disagree? Support your opinion with reasons and examples. Write 200-300 words.
text:
The rapid spread of remote work over the past few years has sparked a debate about whether it truly benefits employees. While working from home offers clear advantages in terms of flexibility and time, I believe that a combination of home and office work is ultimately better for most employees.

On the one hand, remote work eliminates the daily commute, which can consume several hours each week and cause considerable stress. This time can instead be devoted to rest, exercise or family, which in turn may improve wellbeing and job satisfaction. Furthermore, many employees find that they can concentrate more effectively at home, away from the constant interruptions of an open-plan office.

On the other hand, working exclusively from home has notable drawbacks. Employees may feel isolated from their colleagues, and the boundary between work and personal life can easily become blurred, leading to longer working hours rather than shorter ones. In addition, junior staff often miss out on informal learning opportunities, such as observing how senior colleagues handle difficult clients, which are difficult to replicate online.

For these reasons, a hybrid arrangement appears to offer the best of both worlds. Spending two or three days in the office allows employees to collaborate and build relationships, while the remaining days at home provide the flexibility and focus that many value.

In conclusion, although working from home has significant benefits, it is not necessarily better than office work in every respect, and a balanced hybrid model is likely to serve employees most effectively.

prompt: Some people say that working from home is better for employees than working in an office. Do you agree or disagree? Support your opinion with reasons and examples. Write 200-300 words.
text:
Few changes in working life have been as abrupt as the shift to remote work. Although its advocates portray working from home as unambiguously superior, I would argue that its benefits for employees, while genuine, are highly dependent on the nature of the job and the stage of a person's career.

Admittedly, the advantages are substantial. Freed from commuting, employees regain time that can be invested in rest, family or further study, and many report sharper concentration away from the distractions of a shared office. For experienced professionals whose work is largely independent, such as software developers or translators, remote arrangements can therefore raise both productivity and quality of life.

However, these gains are unevenly distributed. Employees early in their careers frequently rely on spontaneous interaction to absorb tacit knowledge, seek quick advice and become visible to managers, all of which are diminished when contact is limited to scheduled video calls. Moreover, those living in small or crowded homes may find that the supposed comfort of remote work translates into cramped, noisy conditions and an erosion of the boundary between professional and private life.

Consequently, the more persuasive position is that flexibility, rather than remote work itself, is what benefits employees. Allowing staff to choose where they work according to their tasks and circumstances captures the advantages of home working without imposing its costs on those it does not suit.

In conclusion, working from home is not inherently better for employees; it is better for some employees, some of the time, and organisations should design their policies accordingly.

prompt: Read the passage below and summarize it using one sentence. Your response should be between 5 and 75 words.
context: Cities are often several degrees warmer than the countryside around them, a phenomenon known as the urban heat island effect. Dark surfaces such as asphalt and rooftops absorb sunlight during the day and release the heat slowly at night, while the lack of vegetation reduces the cooling effect of evaporation. Rising urban temperatures increase energy demand for air conditioning and pose serious risks to elderly residents during heatwaves. Planting street trees is among the most cost-effective responses. Trees shade buildings and pavements, and the water they release through their leaves cools the surrounding air. Studies in several cities have found that streets with dense tree cover can be up to four degrees cooler on summer afternoons than similar streets without trees. However, trees require space, water and maintenance, and many older neighbourhoods have narrow streets and underground pipes that make planting difficult. Urban planners are therefore combining tree planting with other measures, such as reflective roof coatings and green roofs, to reduce heat in areas where trees cannot easily be grown.
